title: Insurance
tagline: What insurance is and how it works, the principles a contract of insurance rests on, and its role in commerce. Unit weight: 10 marks.

overview.intro: Insurance does not remove risk; it reallocates it. A trader who insures a warehouse still faces fire, but the financial consequence moves from her balance sheet to a pool funded by thousands of traders who face the same hazard. That pooling is the whole mechanism, and it only works because the law insists on strict conditions so that one party cannot profit from her own carelessness or her own misfortune. This unit defines insurance and explains its principles, distinguishes the main branches of insurance, and sets out the role insurance plays in commerce by making risk bearable and credit possible.

learningOutcomes: Define insurance and explain the pooling mechanism behind it.
State and apply the principles of insurance.
Distinguish life insurance from fire and marine insurance.
Explain the role of insurance in trade and industry.
Identify what is and is not an insurable risk.

blocks.text: Insurance is a contract in which one party undertakes to indemnify another against loss arising from specified events in return for a payment called the premium. The insured pays a small, certain cost to avoid a large, uncertain one, and the insurer can afford to promise that because it collects premiums from a very large pool of people and can predict how many of them will claim. What insurance transfers is the financial consequence of a risk, not the risk itself: the fire can still occur, but the loss no longer falls on one warehouse owner alone.

items.text: A trader pays ₹20,000 a year to cover stock worth ₹2 crore against fire.
items.note: A small certain payment replaces the threat of a loss that could close the business.

items.text: A shipper insures a consignment for its invoice value plus ten per cent.
items.note: The additional margin reflects the trader’s expectation of profit, which is also an insurable interest.

blocks.text: Six principles carry the doctrine. Utmost good faith requires each party to disclose everything material to the risk, so a proposer who knows a building has faulty wiring must say so. Insurable interest requires the insured to stand to lose from the event insured against, which is why a person cannot insure a stranger’s house. Indemnity holds that the insured should be placed in the same financial position as before the loss, neither better nor worse, and it applies to general insurance though not to life insurance.

blocks.caption: The principles of insurance and their effect
rows: Utmost good faith
Material facts must be disclosed by both sides or the contract is voidable
Insurable interest
The insured must stand to lose from the insured event
Indemnity
Compensation restores the position before the loss, no more
Contribution
Where several policies cover one loss, each pays its share only
Proximate cause
The insurer answers for the nearest effective cause of the loss
Mitigation
The insured must take reasonable steps to limit the loss
Subrogation
After paying, the insurer may pursue the party who caused the loss
Assignment
Rights under a policy may be transferred with the interest insured

blocks.text: Contribution prevents a trader from recovering twice by insuring the same stock with two insurers, and it follows directly from indemnity. Proximate cause decides which policy responds when a chain of events unfolds, such as a fire that starts during an earthquake. Mitigation is an obligation on the insured: a policyholder who watches goods burn without calling the fire brigade has breached her duty even though the fire itself was not her fault.

items.text: A warehouse insured for ₹50 lakh with two insurers covering ₹30 lakh and ₹20 lakh.
items.note: A loss of ₹10 lakh is shared proportionately rather than paid twice, under contribution.

items.text: A ship damaged because a storm drove it onto rocks.
items.note: The proximate cause is the storm, so a policy excluding storms responds differently from one excluding collisions.

blocks.text: Insurance is conventionally divided into life insurance and general insurance, the latter covering fire, marine and miscellaneous risks. Life insurance is not a contract of indemnity, because a life cannot be valued in money and the sum assured is paid on the happening of the event regardless of loss. Fire insurance covers loss or damage to property by fire and perils closely connected with fire. Marine insurance covers the ship, the cargo and the freight against the perils of the sea, and is usually written on an open policy for a year or a voyage policy for one journey.

items: Life insurance includes whole life, endowment and term plans.
Fire insurance covers fire and specified perils, not every source of loss.
Marine insurance covers hull, cargo and freight against sea perils.
Motor, health, burglary and liability cover fall under miscellaneous insurance.

learn.title: The role of insurance in commerce

blocks.text: Insurance supports trade by removing the fear of catastrophe from decisions that commerce needs someone to take. A shipper who cannot insure a consignment will not send it, a factory that cannot insure its building will not borrow against it, and a lender who cannot require insurance will not advance money against goods in a warehouse. Insurance therefore makes credit possible, keeps production continuous after a loss, stabilises the cost of unexpected events for small firms, and encourages risk-taking that benefits the whole economy.

blocks.caption: Where insurance enables a commercial step
rows: Lending against goods or property
The lender requires a policy naming it as payee
Shipping goods overseas
Marine cover lets the exporter pass risk in transit
Continuous production
A loss is recovered instead of ending the business
Employment of labour
Employers’ liability and health cover protect the workforce
New ventures
Founders can attempt more because failure is survivable

items.text: A bank financing a warehouse keeps the policy in its name until the loan is repaid.
items.note: The collateral is protected, which is what makes the advance possible at all.

items.text: A manufacturer recovering within weeks of a fire.
items.note: Without cover, payroll and orders would stop and the firm would rarely reopen.

keyPoints: Insurance is a contract to indemnify against specified loss in return for a premium.
It transfers the financial consequence of risk rather than removing the risk.
A risk must be fortuitous, measurable, accompanied by insurable interest and not self-caused.
Utmost good faith requires disclosure of every material fact by both parties.
Insurable interest must exist at inception and at loss for general insurance.
Indemnity restores the position before the loss and does not apply to life insurance.
Contribution prevents double recovery under several policies.
Proximate cause is the nearest effective cause of the loss.
Mitigation obliges the insured to limit the loss, and subrogation lets the insurer recover afterwards.
Insurance makes credit, shipping and continuous production possible in commerce.
examFocus: Ten marks means naming the principle and applying it to the scenario, since principle questions are always set as situations.
The life and general insurance distinction turns on indemnity and valuation, so state those first.
In role answers, connect each role to a commercial transaction that would otherwise not happen.

questions.prompt: The principle that requires both parties to an insurance contract to disclose all material facts is:
questions.explanation: Utmost good faith governs disclosure, and concealment of a material fact makes the contract voidable at the option of the injured party.

questions.prompt: A trader insures the same stock with two insurers for ₹10 lakh and ₹5 lakh and suffers a loss of ₹3 lakh. The principle applied is:
questions.explanation: Contribution requires each insurer to pay its proportionate share so that the insured recovers the loss once, not twice.

questions.prompt: Which branch of insurance is NOT a contract of indemnity?
questions.explanation: A life has no measurable money value, so the sum assured is paid on the event without any question of restoring a position.

questions.prompt: A fire caused by an earthquake spreads to a neighbouring building. Under a policy covering fire but excluding earthquake, the insurer’s liability depends on:
options: The proximate cause of the loss
Whether a claim was filed promptly
questions.answer: The proximate cause of the loss
questions.explanation: Proximate cause decides which policy responds: if the fire is the effective cause, the fire policy answers even though the fire began during an excluded event.

questions.prompt: The payment made by the insured to obtain the insurer’s undertaking is called the __________ .
questions.explanation: The premium is the consideration without which the contract of insurance has no support.

questions.prompt: The right of an insurer, after paying a claim, to recover from the third party who caused the loss is known as __________ .
questions.explanation: Subrogation lets the insurer step into the insured’s position and pursue the party actually at fault, which keeps premiums down.

questions.prompt: State four principles of insurance and explain any two.
questions.answer: Four principles are utmost good faith, insurable interest, indemnity and contribution, with proximate cause and mitigation also acceptable. Utmost good faith requires each party to disclose every material fact, so a proposer must reveal known hazards such as faulty wiring. Indemnity requires that after a loss the insured be placed in the same financial position as before, neither better nor worse, which is why under-insurance or over-insurance both reduce the recovery. Insurable interest requires the insured to stand to lose from the event, and contribution prevents a claim being recovered twice from two policies.
questions.explanation: Four must be named and two explained, since naming alone earns only part of the marks.

questions.prompt: Distinguish life insurance from fire insurance on three bases.
questions.answer: On nature, life insurance is not a contract of indemnity because no money value can be placed on a life, whereas fire insurance is an indemnity contract measured by the value of property lost. On insurable interest, life insurance requires an interest only at the time the contract is made, while fire insurance requires it both at inception and at the time of the loss. On the number of policies, a life policy can be honoured in full under several contracts, whereas fire policies together pay no more than the actual loss, any excess being recoverable only under the principle of contribution.
questions.explanation: Three bases of comparison are needed, each stated as a contrast rather than a description of one contract.

questions.prompt: Explain any five principles of insurance with the purpose each serves.
questions.answer: Utmost good faith requires full disclosure of material facts by both parties, which prevents one side from contracting on information the other has deliberately withheld. Insurable interest requires the insured to have a stake in the subject matter, so that insurance remains protection rather than gambling. Indemnity limits recovery to the actual loss, placing the insured in the position she occupied before it and removing any incentive to profit from a claim. Contribution applies where more than one policy covers the same risk, so each insurer pays its share and the loss is recovered once. Proximate cause determines which policy responds by identifying the nearest effective cause of the loss. Mitigation obliges the insured to take reasonable steps to limit the damage, so that the insurer’s liability is not increased by carelessness after the event.
questions.explanation: Five principles are required, each with the mischief it prevents, because stating the rule without its purpose earns only partial credit.

questions.prompt: A shopkeeper buys a policy stating the shop is used as a warehouse, when she actually runs a chemical store, and a fire later results from the chemical stock. Analyse the insurer’s position and the duties of the shopkeeper.
questions.answer: The contract has been induced by a misdescription of the material nature of the risk, which breaches the principle of utmost good faith: the use of the premises is exactly the fact that determines both the likelihood and the severity of fire, so it is material and had to be disclosed. Because it was withheld, the insurer may treat the contract as voidable and repudiate the claim, retaining only the right to premiums already received. The shopkeeper’s duty did not end at inception either; a change in the risk, such as converting a shop into a chemical store, must be notified, since the premium was calculated on a different exposure. Separately, the insurer must still establish the proximate cause of the fire: if the chemicals caused it directly, the concealment makes the claim defeasible regardless, while if an unrelated external cause were the proximate cause the same conclusion would follow from the misdescription. The lesson for the proposer is that under-declaring a risk to obtain a lower premium is the fastest route to having no cover at all, and for the insurer it shows why underwriting information is verified before a claim rather than after.
questions.explanation: The answer must identify good faith and materiality, the continuing duty to notify change, and proximate cause as a separate issue, before reaching the conclusion.
